North facing slopes are the most productive sites; however, the majority of these stands presently contain stagnated, doghair thickets of ponderosa pine.
The Northern Cheyenne Inventory data indicate that approximately 13 percent of the present timber volume may be defective. In order of decreasing importance, the major factors contributing to defect are knots, crook, fire scars and interior rot.
The current stumpage received on the Crow Indian Reservation is $25.00 per thousand board feet; with a 90 board foot per acre per year growth, each timbered acre on the project area could return approximately $2.25 per year to the land owner.
Forest areas are now being utilized for domestic livestock grazing, wildlife habitat, recreation, minor harvesting of posts, poles and fire wood, and sawtimber production. The importance of the latter is marginal due to poor quality of the stands and fluctuations in lumber market conditions. Major purchasers of sawtimber in the area include sawmills located at Roundup and Ashland, Montana, and Sheridan, Wyoming.
The Project Area presently contains approximately 32.5 million board feet (3,000 BF/acre) of timber and is producing almost one million board feet annually based on a assumed current growth rate of 90 Bf/acre/year. Based on a sustained yield of one million board feet per year, six man-years (Johnson, 1972) of employment could be created or maintained in the primary processing of this growth.
